messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette failed validation. Make ONLY the targeted changes listed below.

Previous vignette:
Mara, a 19-year-old European American dancer, was in the middle of a crowded late-night performance rehearsal when the disaster happened: a crush of people surged suddenly through an exit corridor, bodies pressed hard against her, and for several terrifying minutes she was pinned, unable to move, with hands gripping her arms and shoulders as others shoved past. The smell of sweat, dust, and hot metal from the backstage equipment was overpowering, and the sensation of being held down while she could not orient herself or get free became the moment she would later return to in fragments. In the aftermath she told herself that what happened was deeply unfair and that nothing had been done about it, and she came to feel that she no longer belonged anywhere. She could not put the event into words easily; when she tried, she knew what had happened but could not find language that felt strong enough or complete enough, which left the memory feeling sealed off and impossible to explain.

At first, the memory would return with alarming force, not as a story but as something completely real across all her senses at once. A sudden recollection of the corridor could bring back the same crushed feeling in her chest, the press of bodies, and even the same smell of sweat and dust, so that she would freeze in place as if it were happening again. The more often that happened, the more certain she became that thinking about it would be unbearable. What frightened her most was that the episode seemed to live in her body as much as in her mind, and that made her avoid any attempt to put it into words. She began to have difficulty concentrating in class and during choreography, because a flash of the memory would take over her attention in the middle of counting steps or listening to a teacher. She also woke during the night to check whether she was safe, lying tense in bed and listening for danger, and she reacted to unexpected movement nearby as if she were in danger, flinching when another dancer crossed too close behind her in the studio.

Those moments of threat made her try to protect herself in the ways that felt immediately available. After the first wave of symptoms, Mara started avoiding going out except when she had to, and even then she planned routes carefully, choosing quieter streets and arriving late to avoid crowds. In class and in public she would sometimes cover her face with her hands, not wanting anyone to see how exposed she felt when she was scared. She also gave up pleasant activities she used to enjoy, including post-rehearsal coffee with other dancers and spontaneous evenings out, because she did not trust herself to stay calm once she left the apartment. Her fear of being followed or tracked intensified these habits; on the walk home from the studio she constantly glanced over her shoulder, certain that someone might be watching her or moving too close behind her. The more she stayed in, the more she felt cut off from the ordinary life she had before, and that sense of not belonging anywhere hardened her conviction that the world outside had become unsafe and alien.

Those strategies brought short-term relief but also kept feeding the problem. Staying home meant she encountered fewer ordinary cues that might have reminded her she was in the present, so the old memory remained ready to erupt with the smallest reminder. When she did go out, she was so alert to being followed, to sudden movement, and to feeling trapped in a crowd that even a crowded sidewalk or a dancer brushing past her shoulder could become a trigger. Her body treated those moments like another threat, and the jumpiness made her watch for danger even more closely. The more she scanned for what might happen next, the more she noticed bodily sensations and environmental details that linked back to the original corridor, and those details could pull the full memory back with unnerving vividness. Being tired became especially potent: after long rehearsal days, when exhaustion lowered her guard, she was more likely to feel the memory coming back, and the same drained state made her more afraid that she would not be able to cope if it hit again. That fear kept her checking the night for safety and helped maintain the cycle of poor sleep, concentration problems, and daytime vigilance.

Over time, Mara began to recognize that she was still living as though the disaster might repeat, and that her world had narrowed around avoiding whatever might remind her of it. She came for help after missing rehearsals and turning down performances she had once wanted badly, frightened that she was losing the life she had built as a dancer. What she most wanted was to feel safe in her own body again and to stop believing that she belonged nowhere, but she was also afraid that if she allowed herself to think about what happened for too long, the memory would overwhelm her completely.

Issues to fix:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette mentions cues or reminders, but it does not clearly say they lead to avoidance or other maladaptive strategies in the same paragraph.
  e.g. "She stopped taking that route to work entirely — better to add twenty minutes to her commute than to feel that way again."
  e.g. "When the anniversary came around, she kept herself moving all day, cleaning, cooking, anything, because sitting still meant the thoughts would catch up."
  e.g. "She started leaving events early, telling herself she was tired, because staying too long meant the chances of something going wrong only multiplied."
- Triggers → Memory: The vignette describes reminders that bring back the memory, but it does not explicitly show triggers causing the traumatic memory to recur in a causal way within one paragraph.
  e.g. "The smell of his cologne in the lift sent the whole night flooding back before she had even reached her floor."
  e.g. "Hearing that song on the radio dragged her straight back into the room where it happened, as if no time had passed at all."
  e.g. "Walking past the bus stop where it occurred, she was no longer on the street — she was back there, every detail sharp and close."
- Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies: The negative beliefs about unfairness and not belonging are present, but the vignette does not directly link them to the avoidance and safety behaviors.
  e.g. "If she had concluded that the world was dangerous and she was defenceless, staying home wasn't avoidance — it was the only rational thing to do."
  e.g. "The belief that speaking about it would make things worse kept her silent in her sessions, offering fragments instead of the whole picture."
  e.g. "Having decided that her feelings couldn't be trusted, she worked hard to stay numb — and had become quite good at it."
- Threat → Triggers: The vignette shows triggers and later threat reactions, but it does not clearly state that perceived threat causes the triggering stimuli in a causal sequence.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Threat: The avoidance and safety behaviors are described as responses to threat, but the vignette does not clearly state that these strategies increase or sustain her sense of threat.
  e.g. "Never having stayed in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, her body had never received the evidence it needed — the threat remained as high as the day it was set."
  e.g. "The checking and the avoidance had kept her alive, in her nervous system's accounting, which meant the danger they were responding to must be real and ongoing."
  e.g. "Without ever testing the feeling, she had no way to know that the threat was not what her body insisted it was — the safety behaviours had sealed that possibility off."

---

Return ONLY patch blocks — do NOT return the full vignette.

For each REQUIRED EDGE MISSING — produce one INSERT_AFTER block.
Find a paragraph in the vignette that already mentions component A, and add a sentence
after it that shows A influencing B through natural clinical language.
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
[copy 1–2 sentences from the vignette — the anchor after which to insert]
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
[one or two sentences that convey A influencing B, written as natural clinical prose]
<<<END>>>

Output ONLY these patch blocks. No prose, no explanation, no full vignette.

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
At first, the memory would return with alarming force, not as a story but as something completely real across all her senses at once. A sudden recollection of the corridor could bring back the same crushed feeling in her chest, the press of bodies, and even the same smell of sweat and dust, so that she would freeze in place as if it were happening again.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Living with that background sense of danger, Mara began reading ordinary things as warnings, and those warnings made the world feel densely packed with reminders she could not stop noticing. A crowded sidewalk, a narrow doorway, or another dancer moving too close behind her could tip straight into alarm, and she would avoid the route, leave the room, or keep herself at the edge of the studio before the fear had time to rise further.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
In the aftermath she told herself that what happened was deeply unfair and that nothing had been done about it, and she came to feel that she no longer belonged anywhere. She could not put the event into words easily; when she tried, she knew what had happened but could not find language that felt strong enough or complete enough, which left the memory feeling sealed off and impossible to explain.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Because she had come to believe the world had failed her and that she did not fit safely anywhere, staying home or slipping away early felt less like avoidance than the only sensible way to protect herself. The same belief that speaking about it would leave her exposed also kept her from telling anyone the whole story, so she offered only fragments and tried to manage it alone.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Those moments of threat made her try to protect herself in the ways that felt immediately available. After the first wave of symptoms, Mara started avoiding going out except when she had to, and even then she planned routes carefully, choosing quieter streets and arriving late to avoid crowds.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Those precautions gave her brief relief, but because she never stayed long enough in the places that frightened her to learn they could pass uneventfully, the sense of danger never loosened. Each time she retreated, her body seemed to take that as confirmation that the threat was still real and still waiting.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
The more often that happened, the more certain she became that thinking about it would be unbearable. What frightened her most was that the episode seemed to live in her body as much as in her mind, and that made her avoid any attempt to put it into words.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Even the smell of sweat in the studio locker room or the sight of an exit corridor at rehearsal could send her straight back to the crush of that night before she had time to orient herself. Once the memory hit, she would pull away from the space, keep her face down, and get out as quickly as she could.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
The more she stayed in, the more she felt cut off from the ordinary life she had before, and that sense of not belonging anywhere hardened her conviction that the world outside had become unsafe and alien.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
That conviction fed the same pattern in reverse: if she was already certain she was alone and unsafe, then avoiding plans, crowds, and even pleasant invitations felt justified, almost necessary. She stopped trusting herself to remain calm once she left the apartment, and the more she withdrew, the more the outside world seemed to prove her fear right.
<<<END>>>
